lead: Two phases of a pure substance coexist in equilibrium only along one curve of the p–T plane, the saturation line. Along it their Gibbs functions are equal. Differentiating that equality gives the slope dp/dT in terms of the latent heat and the volume change: the Clapeyron equation. Its liquid-vapour form with an ideal-gas vapour, the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, turns vapour-pressure readings into latent heats, predicts boiling points, and explains why pressure lowers the melting point of ice.
prereq: You need: dg = v dp − s dT and the equality of Gibbs functions at phase equilibrium from Gibbs and Helmholtz functions, and saturation properties from the steam tables.

sections.h3: Equal Gibbs functions fix the slope of the saturation line

blocks.text: Take a pure substance with two phases, 1 and 2, in equilibrium at p and T. Then g₁ = g₂. Move a small step along the saturation line: T rises by dT and p by dp, and the phases stay in equilibrium, so dg₁ = dg₂. Each phase changes by dg = v dp − s dT:

blocks.where: v₁, s₁ are the specific volume (m³/kg) and entropy (kJ/(kg·K)) of phase 1; v₂, s₂ of phase 2.

blocks.text: Collect terms and use s₁ − s₂ = h₁₂/T, because the phase change happens at constant T and p with reversible heat h₁₂ per kg:

blocks.where: dp/dT is the slope of the saturation line in Pa/K when h₁₂ is in J/kg; h₁₂ is the latent heat; v₁₂ = v₁ − v₂ is the change of specific volume (m³/kg); T is in K.

blocks.text: This is the Clapeyron equation. It makes no ideal-gas assumption and holds for any pair of phases: solid-liquid, liquid-vapour, solid-vapour. Some syllabi call it the Clapeyron equation and keep the name Clausius-Clapeyron for the vapour form below.

sections.h3: The vapour form: ideal gas and small liquid volume

blocks.text: For liquid and vapour, dp/dT = h<sub>fg</sub>/(T·v<sub>fg</sub>) with v<sub>fg</sub> = v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>. Two approximations make it usable with vapour-pressure readings alone. Far below the critical point v<sub>f</sub> ≪ v<sub>g</sub>, so v<sub>fg</sub> ≈ v<sub>g</sub>; and the vapour is close to an ideal gas, v<sub>g</sub> = RT/p, with R the gas constant of the vapour (0.4615 kJ/(kg·K) for steam). Then

blocks.where: This is the Clausius-Clapeyron equation. A plot of ln p against 1/T is nearly straight over a short range, with slope −h<sub>fg</sub>/R in kelvin.

blocks.text: With h<sub>fg</sub> held constant between two states, integration gives the form used in problems:

blocks.where: p₁, T₁ is a known saturation pair and p₂, T₂ the other; both temperatures in K; h<sub>fg</sub>/R is in K, so the right side is a pure number.

sections.h3: Reading the sign: melting lines and boiling lines

blocks.text: For melting, dp/dT = h<sub>sf</sub>/(T·v<sub>sf</sub>), with h<sub>sf</sub> the latent heat of fusion and v<sub>sf</sub> = v<sub>liquid</sub> − v<sub>solid</sub>. Most solids are denser than their liquids, so v<sub>sf</sub> > 0 and pressure raises the melting point.

Water is the standard exception: ice is less dense than water, so v<sub>sf</sub> < 0 and the melting line slopes backwards, about −1.35 × 10⁷ Pa/K. Turned round, dT/dp is about −0.0075 K per atmosphere, so pressure lowers the melting point of ice slightly. This explains regelation: a loaded wire sinks through a block of ice as the ice melts under it, and the water refreezes above it.

On the liquid-vapour line dp/dT is always positive and grows with temperature, so the curve bends upward. A pressure cooker at about 2 bar boils water at a higher temperature and cooks faster; water boils below 100 °C on a mountain. Figure 4.6.1 compares the curve given by the integrated equation with steam-table points.

examples.question: Water boils at T₁ = 373 K where p₁ = 101.3 kPa. Take h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg and R = 0.4615 kJ/(kg·K) for steam. With h<sub>fg</sub> held constant, estimate the saturation pressure at T₂ = 323 K, and explain why it differs from the steam-table value of 12.35 kPa.
steps: Both temperatures are already in kelvin.

The estimate is about 8 % above 12.35 kPa. The real h<sub>fg</sub> rises from 2257 kJ/kg at 373 K to about 2382 kJ/kg at 323 K; using the larger value over part of the range would make the exponent more negative and the pressure lower. The constant-h<sub>fg</sub> assumption is the main error over a 50 K gap.
examples.answer: The estimate is 13.3 kPa, against 12.35 kPa in the steam tables; the gap comes mainly from holding h<sub>fg</sub> constant.

examples.question: At 273.15 K, ice has v = 0.0010908 m³/kg and water v = 0.0010002 m³/kg, and the latent heat of fusion is 333.5 kJ/kg. Find the slope of the melting line and estimate the melting point of ice at 10 MPa.
steps: Reciprocal: dT/dp = −7.42 × 10⁻⁸ K/Pa, which is −0.0075 K per atmosphere (× 101 325 Pa).
Pressure rise from 1 atm to 10 MPa: Δp = 10 000 000 − 101 325 = 9.90 × 10⁶ Pa.
examples.answer: The melting line has dp/dT = −1.35 × 10⁷ Pa/K; at 10 MPa ice melts at about 272.4 K, 0.73 K below the normal melting point.

traps: Using Celsius in the exponent. The integrated form needs kelvin: 50 in place of 323 is nonsense.
Mixing per-kg and per-mole units. 2257 kJ/kg with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) gives an answer far off; use R = 0.4615 kJ/(kg·K) for steam.
Using v<sub>fg</sub> ≈ v<sub>g</sub> with an ideal vapour near the critical point, where v<sub>f</sub> and v<sub>g</sub> are close. Use the full Clapeyron equation with table values there.
Assuming every melting line slopes forward. Ice is the exception: v<sub>sf</sub> < 0, so dp/dT < 0.
Confusing dp/dT (Pa/K) with dT/dp (K/Pa). For ice, dp/dT ≈ −1.35 × 10⁷ Pa/K and dT/dp ≈ −0.0075 K per atmosphere.

quiz.q: State the Clapeyron equation and name every symbol with its unit.
quiz.a: dp/dT = h₁₂/(T·v₁₂): dp/dT is the slope of the saturation line (Pa/K), h₁₂ the latent heat (J/kg), T the absolute temperature (K), v₁₂ the change of specific volume (m³/kg).

quiz.q: For ln p plotted against 1/T, what is the slope and what does it give?
quiz.a: The slope is −h<sub>fg</sub>/R, in K. Multiplying its size by R gives h<sub>fg</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is s₁ − s₂ equal to h₁₂/T for a phase change?
quiz.a: A phase change at fixed pressure happens at constant T, and the reversible heat per kg is h₁₂, so Δs = ∫δq/T = h₁₂/T.

quiz.q: Why does the ice-water melting line slope backwards when most melting lines slope forward?
quiz.a: The slope is h<sub>sf</sub>/(T·v<sub>sf</sub>). Most solids are denser than their liquids, so v<sub>sf</sub> > 0. Ice is less dense than water, so v<sub>sf</sub> < 0 and the slope is negative: pressure lowers its melting point.

quiz.q: Using p₁ = 101.3 kPa at T₁ = 373 K, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg and R = 0.4615 kJ/(kg·K), estimate the saturation pressure at 353 K.
A plot of ln p against 1/T for a vapour has slope −4891 K. Find h<sub>fg</sub> if R = 0.4615 kJ/(kg·K).
The estimate at 323 K came out above the steam-table value. Which assumption is mainly responsible, and which way does it push the answer?
quiz.a: Holding h<sub>fg</sub> constant. The real h<sub>fg</sub> is larger at lower temperature (about 2382 kJ/kg at 323 K), so the true exponent is more negative and the true pressure lower. The estimate therefore overshoots: 13.3 against 12.35 kPa.

beyond: Real vapour-pressure curves are fitted with the Antoine equation, log₁₀ p = A − B/(C + T), with three constants and a wide accurate range; the Wagner equation does better near the critical point. Chemical engineers use these fits to size distillation columns. Search next: Antoine equation, Wagner equation, dew-point calculation.

figure.caption: Saturation pressure of water: the curve is the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation started from 101.3 kPa at 373 K with the latent heat held at 2257 kJ/kg, and the squares are steam-table values. The curve lies a little high at low temperature (13.31 against 12.35 kPa at 323 K), because the real latent heat grows as the temperature falls.
